text:
Agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria) — Commission E Monograph

Agrimony herb (Herba Agrimoniae) is approved by the German Commission E for the symptomatic relief of mild, nonspecific, acute diarrhea and for topical use in mild inflammation of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa. The primary mechanism of action is attributed to its high tannin content (4–10%), particularly the ellagitannin agrimoniin, which exerts astringent [protein-precipitating] effects on mucous membranes, thereby reducing local inflammation and secretion. Accompanying flavonoids may contribute mild antispasmodic and anti-inflammatory activity. Clinical evidence supporting these uses is based principally on traditional use and pharmacological plausibility rather than modern randomized controlled trials; the Commission E assessed the risk-benefit profile as positive for these limited indications.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria). Part used: Herba Agrimoniae. Key constituents: tannins (4–10%, primarily agrimoniin, a condensed ellagitannin), flavonoids (luteolin, apigenin, quercetin glycosides), bitter principles, silicic acid, and trace essential oils.
title: Agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria) — Commission E Monograph

text:
Alder Buckthorn Bark (Frangula alnus) — Commission E Monograph

Alder Buckthorn bark (Cortex Frangulae) is approved by the German Commission E as a short-term treatment for constipation, specifically where easy defecation with a soft stool is desired, such as in cases of anal fissures, hemorrhoids, or post-anorectal surgery. Its laxative action is attributed primarily to anthranoide glycosides — principally glucofrangulines A and B (comprising approximately 60–80% of the total anthranoid fraction) and frangulines A and B — which are hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria to active aglycones that stimulate peristalsis and inhibit water and electrolyte reabsorption in the large intestine, thereby softening the stool and accelerating transit. Clinical and pharmacological evidence supports efficacy consistent with other anthraquinone-based stimulant laxatives; the Commission E endorses use only for short-term relief (generally no longer than 1–2 weeks) due to risks of electrolyte imbalance, hypokalemia, and potential for laxative dependency with prolonged use. Fresh bark must be stored for at least one year (or subjected to heat treatment) before use, as freshly dried bark contains frangula-emodin anthrone and related compounds that cause nausea and vomiting.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: (1) Comminuted bark as a decoction or cold-water macerate for oral use; (2) Dry extract preparations in tablets or capsules; (3) Liquid preparations (tinctures, fluid extracts). Recommended daily dose: 20–30 mg hydroxyanthracene derivatives, calculated as glucofrangulin A, taken in the evening. The minimum effective dose should always be used. Duration of use should not exceed 1–2 weeks without medical supervision. The bark must be stored for a minimum of one year, or alternatively subjected to accelerated aging via heat treatment (e.g., heating at 100°C with steam or dry heat for defined periods) before medicinal use to eliminate emetic anthrone compounds.
Indication: Short-term treatment of constipation; facilitation of defecation where soft stools are medically indicated (e.g., hemorrhoids, anal fissures, post-surgical anorectal conditions).

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Alder Buckthorn (Frangula alnus). Part used: Cortex Frangulae (dried bark of Frangula alnus Mill., syn. Rhamnus frangula L.). Key active compounds: Anthranoide, hauptsächlich Glucofranguline A und B (ca. 60–80% der Gesamtanthranoidfraktion) und Franguline A und B; Gesamtanthranoidgehalt mindestens 7,0% (berechnet als Glucofrangulin A, bezogen auf die getrocknete Droge).
title: Alder Buckthorn Bark (Frangula alnus) — Commission E Monograph

text:
Aloe Vera Gel (Aloe barbadensis) — Topical Wound and Skin Preparation

Aloe vera gel, derived from the inner leaf parenchyma of Aloe barbadensis Miller, is approved by the German Commission E for topical use in the supportive treatment of minor burns (including sunburn), skin abrasions, and superficial wounds. Its primary active constituents — notably the high-molecular-weight polysaccharide acemannan — are understood to exert anti-inflammatory, moisturising, and wound-healing effects by inhibiting bradykinin activity, modulating prostaglandin synthesis, and promoting fibroblast proliferation. The gel creates a protective, hydrating film over damaged skin that reduces transepidermal water loss and may accelerate re-epithelialisation. Clinical evidence at the time of Commission E assessment was considered sufficient to support these topical indications, though the monograph did not extend approval to internal use of the gel.

Preparation: Topical application only (per Commission E approval). The gel is used as: (1) fresh cut leaf pulp applied directly to affected skin; (2) stabilised gel preparations (cream, lotion, gel formulation) standardised to contain a minimum of 10–70% Aloe vera inner leaf gel, applied liberally to affected area 2–3 times daily as needed. No specific internal dosage form is approved under this monograph. Preparations should be free of anthraquinone contaminants (aloin <10 ppm in topical products is the general benchmark consistent with Commission E intent).
Indication: Minor first- and second-degree burns; sunburn; superficial skin abrasions; dry, irritated, or minor wounded skin requiring a soothing, moisturising, and wound-supportive topical agent.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Aloe vera gel (Aloe barbadensis). Part used: Aloe Gel [Aloe Gel]. Key constituents: polysaccharides (chiefly acemannan), glycoproteins, anthraquinone-free inner leaf parenchyma gel, enzymes (bradykinase), salicylates, sterols, saponins, and amino acids.
title: Aloe Vera Gel (Aloe barbadensis) — Topical Wound and Skin Preparation

text:
Angelica Root (Angelica archangelica)

Angelica root (Radix Angelicae) is approved by the German Commission E for the treatment of mild gastrointestinal complaints, including feelings of fullness [Völlegefühl], flatulence [Meteorismus], and mild gastrointestinal spasms. It is also indicated for loss of appetite [Appetitlosigkeit]. The essential oil and bitter principles are thought to act as carminative and spasmolytic agents, stimulating gastric secretion and motility through reflex mechanisms in the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical evidence is largely based on traditional use and pharmacological plausibility rather than controlled clinical trials; no contraindications other than known allergy and photosensitivity risk (due to furanocoumarins) are noted.

Preparation: Commission E-approved preparations include: (1) Comminuted [cut] root as a tea infusion or decoction: 4.5 g of dried root per day (single dose approximately 1–1.5 g per cup, taken 2–3 times daily before meals); (2) Tincture (1:5 in 45–70% ethanol): equivalent daily dose corresponding to 4.5 g of dried root; (3) Dry extract and other galenical preparations in corresponding doses. Preparations are typically taken 30 minutes before meals to maximise appetite-stimulating and digestive effects.
Indication: Mild gastrointestinal disorders including loss of appetite, feelings of fullness, flatulence, and mild gastrointestinal spasms [dyspeptic complaints].

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Angelica root (Angelica archangelica). Part used: Radix Angelicae. Key active compounds: essential oil (0.3–1.0%, including α-pinene, β-phellandrene, and macrocyclic lactones), furanocoumarins (including bergapten, xanthotoxin, isoimperatorin), hydroxycoumarins, bitter principles (archangelicin), tannins, and plant acids.
title: Angelica Root (Angelica archangelica)

text:
Anise Fruit (Pimpinella anisum) — German Commission E Monograph

The dried ripe fruit of Pimpinella anisum (Fructus Anisi) is approved by the German Commission E for the relief of dyspeptic complaints such as mild gastrointestinal spasms, feelings of fullness, and flatulence, as well as for catarrhs of the upper respiratory tract. The primary mechanism of action is attributed to the essential oil, particularly trans-anethole, which exerts antispasmodic effects on smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract and acts as an expectorant by increasing bronchial secretion and promoting mucociliary clearance. Clinical use is supported by a long tradition of therapeutic application and pharmacological data consistent with these activities, though large-scale controlled clinical trials are limited. The Commission E assessed the benefit-risk profile as positive for these indications at recommended doses.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Anise (Pimpinella anisum). Part used: Fructus Anisi (dried ripe fruit). Key active compounds: essential oil (minimum 2% per pharmacopoeia standard), comprising principally trans-anethole (80–90%), with minor constituents including estragole (methyl chavicol), pseudoisoeugenol, and anise ketone (p-methoxyphenylacetone).
title: Anise Fruit (Pimpinella anisum) — German Commission E Monograph

text:
Arnica Flower (Arnica montana) — Commission E Monograph Entry

Arnica flower is approved by the German Commission E for external use in the treatment of injuries and their sequelae, such as haematomas, contusions, sprains, and bruising, as well as for symptomatic relief of rheumatic muscle and joint pain, inflammation caused by insect bites, superficial phlebitis, furuncles, and oedema from fractures. Its principal mechanism of action is attributed to the sesquiterpene lactone helenalin and its ester derivatives, which inhibit the transcription factor NF-κB, thereby suppressing the release of pro-inflammatory mediators including prostaglandins and cytokines, producing anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and mild antiseptic effects. Flavonoids contribute additional antioxidant and capillary-stabilising activity, supporting the resolution of haematomas and reduction of local oedema. Clinical and experimental evidence supports topical efficacy at standardised concentrations; internal use is not approved due to toxicity risks and is associated with adverse cardiac and gastrointestinal effects at therapeutic doses.

Preparation: Topical use only (Commission E does not approve internal therapeutic use). Approved dosage forms and doses: (1) Tincture (Arnicae tinctura, per DAB/Ph. Eur.): prepared 1:10 in 70% ethanol from dried flower heads; applied undiluted for compresses or diluted 3–10× with water for poultices and rinses. (2) Semi-solid preparations (creams, gels, ointments): contain 10–25% arnica tincture, or 15% arnica oil (1:5 in fatty oil), or standardised to minimum 0.15% sesquiterpene lactones calculated as dihydrohelenalin tiglate; applied to affected area 2–3 times daily. (3) Mouthwash/gargle: tincture diluted 10× with water for oral mucosal inflammation (not swallowed). Duration: until symptoms resolve; prolonged use on broken skin or in individuals with Asteraceae sensitivity is contraindicated.
Indication: ['Haematomas and bruising (post-traumatic)', 'Contusions and sprains', 'Oedema associated with fractures', 'Rheumatic muscle and joint pain (topical symptomatic relief)', 'Superficial phlebitis', 'Inflammation from insect bites', 'Furuncles (superficial)', 'Oral and pharyngeal mucosal inflammation (gargle, topical)']

Original: Flos Arnicae (Arnica montana L., Asteraceae). Active constituents: sesquiterpene lactones (helenalin and dihydrohelenalin esters, collectively 0.2–0.8% of dry weight), flavonoids (isoquercitrin, astragalin, luteolin glycosides, ~0.4–0.6%), essential oils (~0.2–0.35%), phenolic acids (chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid), carotenoids, tannins, and polysaccharides.
title: Arnica Flower (Arnica montana) — Commission E Monograph Entry

text:
Artichoke Leaf (Cynara scolymus) — German Commission E Monograph

The German Commission E approved artichoke leaf (Folium Cynarae) for the treatment of dyspeptic complaints, including a sense of fullness, flatulence, nausea, abdominal pain, and disorders of fat metabolism. The primary mechanism of action involves stimulation of bile secretion (choleretic effect) by the liver and gallbladder, attributed chiefly to caffeoylquinic acids such as cynarin and chlorogenic acid derivatives, which facilitate fat digestion and support hepatic function. Commission E monographs additionally recognize hepatoprotective properties, with cynarin and related polyphenols demonstrated in in vitro and animal studies to promote liver cell regeneration and reduce oxidative stress; controlled clinical evidence in humans, while supportive, was considered limited at the time of monograph publication. The approved preparation is a standardized dried leaf extract, typically administered orally as an aqueous or hydroalcoholic extract, with the recommended daily dose of 6 g of the dried herb or equivalent extract preparations (standardized to caffeoylquinic acid content).

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Artichoke (Cynara scolymus). Part used: Folium Cynarae (artichoke leaf). Key active compounds: caffeoylquinic acids (including cynarin [1,3-dicaffeoylquinic acid]), flavonoids (luteolin-7-glucoside), sesquiterpene lactones (cynaropicrin), and hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives. Total caffeoylquinic acid content typically 0.5–1.0% in dried leaf material.
title: Artichoke Leaf (Cynara scolymus) — German Commission E Monograph

text:
Asparagus Root

Asparagus root is approved by the German Commission E as an irrigation therapy [Durchspülungstherapie] for inflammatory diseases of the lower urinary tract and for the prevention and treatment of kidney gravel [Nierengrieß]. Its diuretic action is attributed primarily to the amino acid asparagine combined with high potassium content and saponin constituents, which increase renal tubular filtration and urine volume, thereby flushing the urinary tract mechanically. Clinical evidence supporting this indication is based on traditional use and pharmacological plausibility rather than large-scale randomised controlled trials; the Commission E assessed the benefit-risk ratio as positive for the irrigation indication. Asparagus root preparations are contraindicated where increased fluid intake is inadvisable, such as in oedema due to impaired cardiac or renal function, and should not be used in cases of inflammatory kidney disease [Nierenerkrankungen entzündlicher Art].

Original: Radix Asparagi — Asparagus officinalis L. (family Asparagaceae). Key constituents: steroidal saponins (including asparasaponins), flavonoids (rutin, kaempferol glycosides), asparagine (free amino acid), essential oils, polysaccharides (fructooligosaccharides), and hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives. Potassium content notably high, supporting osmotic diuretic activity.
title: Asparagus Root

text:
Lemon Balm Leaf

German Commission E approves lemon balm leaf [Folium Melissae] for the treatment of nervous sleeping disorders and functional gastrointestinal complaints, including nervous stomach upset and flatulence. The volatile oil fraction, particularly citral and citronellal, is believed to exert mild sedative and antispasmodic [spasmolytic] effects on smooth muscle, while rosmarinic acid and flavonoid constituents contribute to anxiolytic and antiviral activity. Clinical and pharmacological evidence supports a calming effect on the central nervous system and a relaxing action on the gastrointestinal tract, though the overall evidence base is characterized as empirically sound rather than derived from large-scale controlled trials. Commission E regards the herb as an approved [positiv bewertet] remedy within these indications at standard therapeutic doses.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E Monographs: (1) Infusion (tea): 1.5–4.5 g of dried leaf per 150 mL water, taken as a single dose, several times daily as needed; (2) Liquid preparations (tinctures, extracts, fluid extracts): equivalent doses standardized to the dried herb; (3) Combination preparations with other approved sedative or carminative herbs are permitted. For sleep disorders, a dose is taken 30 minutes before bedtime. Daily dose: 8–10 g dried herb or equivalent preparations.
Indication: 1. Nervous sleeping disorders (insomnia of nervous origin); 2. Functional gastrointestinal complaints (nervous stomach upset, bloating, flatulence, gastrointestinal spasm)

Original: Folium Melissae (Melissa officinalis L., Lamiaceae). Key active constituents: volatile essential oil (0.02–0.3%) containing citral (geranial and neral), citronellal, and linalool; hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives including rosmarinic acid; flavonoids; and tannins.
title: Lemon Balm Leaf

text:
Bearberry Leaf

Bearberry leaf (Folium Uvae Ursi) is approved by the German Commission E for the treatment of inflammatory conditions of the lower urinary tract and for uncomplicated urinary tract infections. Its primary mechanism of action depends on the hydrolysis of arbutin in alkaline urine to release hydroquinone, which exerts antimicrobial and antiseptic effects on the urinary mucosa; efficacy is therefore greatest when urinary pH is alkaline (above 8). The high tannin content additionally contributes astringent and anti-inflammatory properties on the urinary tract epithelium. Clinical use is supported by in vitro antimicrobial evidence and traditional therapeutic application, though large-scale randomised controlled trials remain limited; the Commission E endorses short-term use (up to one week) and recommends against prolonged or repeated courses due to the hepatotoxic potential of free hydroquinone.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: aqueous infusion (tea) prepared from dried bearberry leaves; standardised dry extracts in tablet or capsule form. Recommended daily dose: 400–840 mg of arbutin (corresponding to 10 g of dried leaf or equivalent extract), administered in divided doses. Preparations should ideally be taken with alkalinising agents (e.g., sodium bicarbonate or a diet rich in alkaline foods) to raise urinary pH and maximise hydroquinone release. Duration of use should not exceed one week, and repeated courses within a single year should be avoided.
Indication: Inflammatory conditions of the lower urinary tract; uncomplicated bacterial urinary tract infections (cystitis); urinary tract discomfort with burning and frequent urination.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Bearberry leaf (Arctostaphylos uva-ursi). Part used: Folium Uvae Ursi. Key active compounds: arbutin (hydroquinone glucoside, 6–12%), methylarbutin, hydroquinone, tannins (gallotannins, ellagitannins, 15–20%), flavonoids (hyperoside, isoquercitrin), iridoids, triterpenes (ursolic acid, uvaol), and allantoin.
title: Bearberry Leaf

text:
Bilberry Fruit (Vaccinium myrtillus) — German Commission E Monograph

Bilberry fruit (Fructus Myrtilli), the dried ripe berry of Vaccinium myrtillus L. (Ericaceae), is approved by the German Commission E for the symptomatic treatment of nonspecific acute diarrhea and for mild inflammation of the mucous membranes of the mouth and throat. The therapeutic action of the dried fruit in diarrhea is attributed primarily to its high tannin content (catechins and proanthocyanidins), which exert astringent [tannin-mediated protein-precipitating] effects on the intestinal mucosa, reducing secretion and inhibiting pathogenic adhesion; pectin contributes an additional mild adsorptive and bulking effect. The anthocyanosides present in both fresh and dried fruit demonstrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and capillary-stabilising properties, and have been associated in clinical and pharmacological studies with improved microcirculatory perfusion and reduced vascular permeability, supporting traditional use for visual and circulatory complaints, though Commission E formal approval for ophthalmological indications was not granted in the primary monograph. The Commission E assessed the dried fruit preparation as clinically efficacious and safe for the approved indications when used at recommended doses; adverse effects are not known at therapeutic doses of the dried berry.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Bilberry fruit (Vaccinium myrtillus). Part used: Fructus Myrtilli. Key active compounds: Anthocyanosides (anthocyanins, primarily delphinidin, cyanidin, petunidin, peonidin, and malvidin glycosides), approximately 0.1–0.25% in fresh fruit and up to 1% in dried fruit; tannins (catechins and proanthocyanidins); pectin; organic acids (citric, malic); vitamins (C, B1, B2); and trace minerals.
title: Bilberry Fruit (Vaccinium myrtillus) — German Commission E Monograph

text:
Birch Leaf

Birch leaf (Folium Betulae) is approved by the German Commission E for use as an aquaretic [irrigation therapy] to support the treatment of bacterial and inflammatory conditions of the lower urinary tract and for the prevention and treatment of kidney gravel [Nierengrieß]. Its mechanism of action is primarily attributed to its pronounced diuretic (aquaretic) effect, which increases urine volume without significant electrolyte loss, thereby flushing the urinary tract; this effect is associated with the flavonoid and saponin content in conjunction with the leaf's naturally high potassium levels. The Commission E considers its use well-established based on traditional and pharmacological evidence, with the increased urine flow mechanically reducing bacterial colonisation and the aggregation of urinary crystalline material. It is also indicated adjunctively for rheumatic complaints, where the increased renal elimination of metabolic waste products is considered therapeutically relevant.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: dried leaf as an infusion (tea), fluid extract, or other galenical preparations for oral use. Recommended daily dose: 2–3 g of the dried leaf as an infusion (tea), taken 2–3 times daily; fluid extract equivalent doses are used correspondingly. Adequate fluid intake (minimum 2 litres of liquid per day) is required to achieve the aquaretic effect. Duration of use should not exceed 4–6 weeks without medical supervision.
Indication: Irrigation therapy [Durchspülungstherapie] for bacterial and inflammatory urinary tract conditions; prevention and treatment of kidney gravel [urolithiasis prophylaxis]; adjunctive treatment of rheumatic complaints.

Original: Folium Betulae (Birch leaf, Betula pendula Roth [syn. Betula alba L., Betula verrucosa Ehrh.]). Key active compounds: flavonoids (hyperoside, quercetin glycosides, myricetin derivatives), hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives, tannins, essential oils, saponins, ascorbic acid, betuloside (arbutin precursor), and high potassium content facilitating aquaretic effect.
title: Birch Leaf

text:
Bishop Weed (Ammi visnaga) — Fruit

The dried ripe fruit of Ammi visnaga (Fructus Ammi Visnagae) is approved by the German Commission E for the supportive treatment of mild spastic conditions of the coronary arteries [leichte spastische Beschwerden der Koronararterien] and for mild forms of obstructive airway disease [leichte Formen obstruktiver Atemwegserkrankungen]. The principal active chromones — khellin and visnagin — exert spasmolytic (smooth-muscle-relaxing) effects on bronchial, coronary, and urinary tract musculature without significant negative inotropic action; visnagin and visnadin additionally contribute to mild coronary vasodilation. Khellin served historically as the structural template for the development of cromoglicic acid (sodium cromoglycate) and the calcium-channel blocker nifedipine, underscoring the pharmacological plausibility of the monograph's indications. Clinical evidence reviewed by the Commission E was judged sufficient to support efficacy for these indications at the recommended doses, though the Commission also noted photosensitisation risk attributable to the furocoumarin constituents.

Preparation: Oral administration of standardised preparations (powdered drug, dry extract, or tincture) providing a daily dose equivalent to 15–30 mg of khellin. The Commission E specifies an average single dose of the crude drug corresponding to approximately 15 mg khellin; total daily dose should not exceed 30 mg khellin. Proprietary standardised preparations (e.g., tablets, capsules, or oral solutions) should be used in preference to non-standardised crude-drug preparations to ensure consistent khellin delivery. Duration of use should be limited and use discontinued if photosensitivity reactions occur.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Bishop weed (Ammi visnaga). Part used: Fructus Ammi Visnagae. Active constituents: Chromones (khellin and visnagin, collectively 0.3–1.5% by dry weight of fruit); furocoumarins (xanthotoxin, bergapten, isopimpinellin); pyranocoumarins (visnadin, samidin, dihydrosamidin); flavonoids; fixed oils.
title: Bishop Weed (Ammi visnaga) — Fruit

text:
Black Cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa) — Rhizome

Black cohosh rhizome (Rhizoma Cimicifugae) is approved by the German Commission E for the relief of climacteric [menopausal] complaints, including hot flushes, profuse perspiration, sleep disturbances, and depressive mood states associated with menopause, as well as for premenstrual syndrome and dysmenorrhoea [painful menstruation]. Its mechanism of action was historically attributed to selective oestrogen receptor modulation, but current evidence suggests the triterpene glycosides act primarily on serotonergic and dopaminergic pathways in the central nervous system rather than through direct oestrogenic activity, explaining its efficacy on vasomotor and mood-related symptoms without stimulating oestrogen-sensitive tissues. Clinical trials, including several randomised controlled studies reviewed by Commission E, support a statistically significant reduction in the Kupperman Menopausal Index scores relative to placebo. The Commission E positive monograph endorses short-term use (up to six months), noting that longer-term safety data were insufficient at the time of monograph publication.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per Commission E: oral preparations including solid dosage forms (tablets, capsules) and liquid preparations (tinctures, fluid extracts). Recommended daily dose: crude drug equivalent of 40 mg of the dried rhizome, or preparations standardised to contain the equivalent of 40 mg crude drug (commonly expressed as 2.5% triterpene glycosides calculated as 27-deoxyactein, yielding approximately 1 mg triterpenes per 40 mg dose). Proprietary standardised extracts (e.g., Remifemin® isopropanolic extract) were used in the majority of clinical studies at a dose of 20 mg extract twice daily. Duration of use: up to 6 months without medical supervision; longer use requires physician oversight.
Indication: Climacteric (menopausal) complaints — hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, depressive mood; premenstrual syndrome (PMS); dysmenorrhoea

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa). Part used: Rhizoma Cimicifugae. Key active constituents include triterpene glycosides (principally actein and 27-deoxyactein; total triterpenes typically standardised to 2.5% calculated as 27-deoxyactein), isoflavones (formononetin, though its presence is now disputed in modern analyses), resinous constituents (cimicifugin/macrotys resin), and isoferulic acid.
title: Black Cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa) — Rhizome

text:
Black Elder Flower (Sambucus nigra) — Commission E Monograph

Black elder flower (Flores Sambuci), derived from Sambucus nigra L. (family Adoxaceae, formerly Caprifoliaceae), is approved by the German Commission E for use as a diaphoretic [sweat-promoting agent] in the supportive treatment of colds. The flowers contain flavonoids (including rutin and isoquercitrin), phenolic acids (chlorogenic acid), mucilages, and volatile compounds that are believed to promote perspiration and support mucous membrane function during upper respiratory infections. Commission E recognizes the traditional use of elder flower preparations — typically consumed as a hot infusion — to induce sweating and thereby aid in the symptomatic relief of feverish colds. Clinical evidence is primarily based on traditional use and pharmacological plausibility rather than controlled clinical trials.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Black elder flower (Sambucus nigra). Part used: Flores Sambuci.
title: Black Elder Flower (Sambucus nigra) — Commission E Monograph

text:
Bogbean Leaf

Bogbean leaf [Folium Menyanthidis] is approved by the German Commission E as a bitter tonic for the treatment of digestive complaints, particularly loss of appetite and dyspeptic symptoms. The bitter principles, primarily iridoid glycosides such as foliamenthin and menyanthin, stimulate gustatory receptors and reflex secretion of saliva and gastric juices, thereby promoting appetite and enhancing digestion. Clinical evidence supporting efficacy is based primarily on traditional use and pharmacological data consistent with the recognized bitter tonic mechanism; controlled clinical trials are limited. The Commission E notes no known risks at recommended therapeutic doses, though large overdoses may cause vomiting and diarrhea.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: (1) Dried leaf as a tea infusion — average daily dose 1.5–3 g of the dried herb, prepared as an infusion (steep 1.5–3 g in 150 mL boiling water for 5–10 minutes), taken 30 minutes before meals; (2) Fluid extract or tincture — equivalent preparations standardized to bitter value; (3) Powdered herb in solid dosage forms. The preparation should deliver a sufficient bitter value consistent with pharmacopoeial standards. Typical course of use: short-term, as needed for appetite stimulation or digestive support.
Indication: Loss of appetite [anorexia]; dyspeptic complaints including bloating, mild gastrointestinal discomfort, and sluggish digestion. Approved as a bitter tonic [Amarum].

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Bogbean (Menyanthes trifoliata). Part used: Folium Menyanthidis (bogbean leaf). Key constituents: iridoid glycosides (including foliamenthin, dihydrofoliamenthin, and menthiafolin), flavonoids (rutin, hyperoside, trifolioside), phenylpropanoid esters, bitter principles (menyanthin), and small amounts of alkaloids and tannins.
title: Bogbean Leaf

text:
Boldo Leaf

Boldo leaf [Folium Boldo] is approved by the German Commission E for mild, spasmodic gastrointestinal complaints and dyspeptic conditions, particularly where sluggish bile flow [dyspepsia of hepatobiliary origin] is implicated. The primary alkaloid boldine exerts choleretic (bile-stimulating) and mild antispasmodic effects on the smooth musculature of the gastrointestinal tract, while the volatile oil constituent ascaridole may contribute to stomachic and carminative activity. Clinical evidence in support of these uses rests largely on traditional use and pharmacological data; robust controlled clinical trials are limited, and the Commission E's positive monograph reflects well-documented empirical use rather than high-level clinical evidence. Due to the hepatotoxic and nephrotoxic potential of ascaridole and certain alkaloids, use is restricted to short-term administration at approved doses.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: dried leaf for infusion (tea), fluid extract, and dry extract in solid dosage forms (capsules, tablets). Recommended daily dose: 3 g of dried leaf as an infusion (tea), or equivalent preparations — fluid extract (1:1 in 45% ethanol): 0.1–0.3 mL three times daily; dry extract standardised preparations dosed equivalently. Duration of use should be limited; the Commission E does not recommend use beyond several weeks without medical supervision. Preparations with significantly elevated ascaridole content should be avoided.
Indication: Mild spasmodic gastrointestinal complaints; dyspeptic disorders involving insufficient bile secretion [hepatobiliary dyspepsia]; general digestive complaints with sluggishness of the upper gastrointestinal tract.

Original: Folium Boldo (Boldo leaf); derived from Peumus boldus Molina (Monimiaceae). Key active constituents: volatile oil (approx. 2%), containing ascaridole (up to 30–40% of oil fraction); alkaloids (approx. 0.2–0.5%), principally boldine; flavonoids including isorhamnetin and kaempferol glycosides.
title: Boldo Leaf

text:
Borage Flower

The German Commission E evaluated borage flower (Flos Boraginis) and ultimately issued a negative monograph, meaning no therapeutic application was formally approved for the flower preparation. The primary safety concern identified was the presence of pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs), which are hepatotoxic and potentially carcinogenic compounds, even at trace concentrations found in the flowers. Although traditional use attributed diaphoretic [sweat-inducing], diuretic, and expectorant properties to borage flower preparations, the Commission E found insufficient clinical evidence to support efficacy for any indication, and the potential risk from PA content was deemed to outweigh unproven therapeutic benefit. Consumers and practitioners are cautioned against internal use of borage flower preparations due to the PA risk; borage seed oil (from Borago officinalis seeds), which is PA-free and rich in gamma-linolenic acid, is regulated separately and is not subject to this negative assessment.

Preparation: No approved therapeutic preparation or dosage is recommended by the German Commission E for Flos Boraginis (borage flower) due to the negative monograph status. Internal use is not sanctioned. Note: Borage seed oil (not covered by this monograph) is used separately at doses typically ranging from 1–3 g/day of gamma-linolenic acid in commercial preparations, but this falls outside the scope of the flower monograph.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Borage (Borago officinalis). Part used: Flos Boraginis (borage flower). Key active compounds: mucilages, tannins, pyrrolizidine alkaloids (trace amounts, including thesinine and intermedine), flavonoids, and silicic acid.
title: Borage Flower

text:
Buchu Leaf

Buchu leaf (Folium Bucco), derived from Agathosma betulina, was evaluated by the German Commission E, which concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support its traditional uses as a urinary tract disinfectant and diuretic. The volatile oil fraction — particularly diosphenol and pulegone — was historically credited with mild antiseptic and diuretic activity in the lower urinary tract, and flavonoids such as diosmin were associated with anti-inflammatory effects. However, the Commission E issued a negative monograph, finding that the claimed efficacy for urinary tract infections, kidney and bladder conditions, and as a diuretic had not been substantiated by adequate clinical evidence. Use of buchu leaf preparations is therefore not recommended under the Commission E framework for any approved therapeutic indication.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Buchu leaf (Agathosma betulina). Part used: Folium Bucco. Key active compounds: volatile oil (1.0–3.5%), diosphenol, pulegone, isopulegone, flavonoids (diosmin, rutin), mucilage, resin.
title: Buchu Leaf

text:
Buckwheat Herb

Buckwheat herb (Herba Fagopyri), derived from Fagopyrum esculentum, is approved by the German Commission E for supportive treatment of chronic venous insufficiency, including symptoms such as pain and heaviness in the legs, nocturnal leg cramps, itching, and swelling. Its principal active constituent, rutin, is a flavonoid glycoside that exerts a vascular-protective effect by reducing capillary fragility and permeability, thereby improving microcirculatory function in peripheral vessels. Clinical evidence supports the use of rutin-containing preparations in managing the oedema and discomfort associated with venous stasis and related circulatory disorders. The Commission E endorsed buckwheat herb preparations standardised for rutin content as a phlebotonic and capillary-stabilising agent.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Buckwheat herb (Fagopyrum esculentum). Part used: Herba Fagopyri. Key active compounds: Rutin (flavonoid glycoside, primarily responsible for therapeutic activity); total flavonoid content variable by preparation.
title: Buckwheat Herb

text:
Butcher's Broom Rhizome (Ruscus aculeatus)

The rhizome of Ruscus aculeatus (Butcher's Broom) is approved by the German Commission E for the symptomatic relief of discomfort and heaviness in the legs associated with chronic venous insufficiency [chronische Veneninsuffizienz], and as a supportive treatment for hemorrhoids [Hämorrhoidalleiden]. The primary mechanism of action is attributed to the steroidal saponins—ruscogenin and neoruscogenin—which exert a venotonic effect by stimulating alpha-adrenergic receptors in the smooth muscle of venous walls, thereby reducing venous distensibility and improving venous return. Anti-inflammatory and vasoconstrictive properties further contribute to reduction of capillary permeability and edema formation in the lower extremities. Clinical evidence supports modest but consistent benefit in reducing symptoms such as leg swelling, itching, tension, and cramping when used as a standardized extract, particularly in combination with hesperidin and ascorbic acid.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs
Plant: Butcher's Broom (Ruscus aculeatus)
Part used: Rhizoma Rusci
Key active compounds: Steroidal saponins (ruscogenins, principally neoruscogenin and ruscogenin), flavonoids (rutin, hesperidin), sparteine alkaloids (trace). Saponin content typically 1–3% of dry rhizome weight.
title: Butcher's Broom Rhizome (Ruscus aculeatus)

text:
Butterbur Herb (Petasites hybridus) — Commission E Monograph

The German Commission E evaluated Herba Petasitidis — the dried aerial parts of Petasites hybridus (butterbur) — and issued a negative monograph, meaning it did not approve therapeutic use of the unprocessed herb due to insufficient evidence of efficacy and the documented presence of hepatotoxic and potentially carcinogenic unsaturated pyrrolizidine alkaloids [uPAs]. The spasmolytic and anti-inflammatory activity observed preclinically is attributed primarily to the sesquiterpene esters petasin and isopetasin, which inhibit leukotriene synthesis and smooth-muscle spasm; however, these benefits were considered insufficient to outweigh the hepatotoxic risk of the unrefined herb. Commission E therefore concluded that, in the unprocessed herb form, the risks outweigh the demonstrated benefits, and therapeutic use cannot be recommended without pyrrolizidine-alkaloid-free standardised extracts. Subsequent post-Commission E research using PA-free standardised root extracts (e.g., Petadolex®) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in migraine prophylaxis and allergic rhinitis, but these findings fall outside the original Commission E negative assessment of Herba Petasitidis.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Butterbur (Petasites hybridus). Part used: Herba Petasitidis (the aerial herb of Petasites hybridus). Key active compounds: petasin and isopetasin (sesquiterpene esters, primary spasmolytic constituents); pyrrolizidine alkaloids (hepatotoxic, present as contaminants in unprocessed material); volatile oils; flavonoids.
title: Butterbur Herb (Petasites hybridus) — Commission E Monograph

text:
Calendula (Pot Marigold) Flower

The German Commission E approves Calendula flower (Flos Calendulae) for the topical treatment of wounds that are slow to heal [poorly healing wounds], including cuts, abrasions, and ulcers, as well as for inflammatory conditions of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa. Its therapeutic activity is attributed primarily to anti-inflammatory, vulnerary [wound-healing], and mildly antimicrobial properties, mediated by flavonoids, triterpene saponins, and carotenoids that promote granulation tissue formation and epithelial regeneration. Clinical and experimental evidence supports its use as a topical agent to reduce local inflammation and accelerate tissue repair, though large-scale randomized controlled trials remain limited. Internal use is additionally approved for inflammation of the gastric and intestinal mucosa, and as a cholagogue [bile-stimulating agent] to support hepatobiliary function.

Preparation: Topical: Infusion (1–2 g of dried flower heads per 150 mL boiling water, steeped 5–10 minutes), used as a compress, rinse, or mouthwash; tincture (1:5 in 70% ethanol), diluted 1:3 to 1:5 with water for topical application; semi-solid preparations (creams, ointments, gels) containing 2–5% dried extract or equivalent. Internal: Infusion of 1–4 g dried flowers in 150 mL water, taken 2–3 times daily between meals; tincture 1–4 mL (1:5, 70% ethanol) up to three times daily. Commission E does not specify a maximum daily dose for topical use; internal use should not exceed 4 g dried herb per single dose.
Indication: Poorly healing wounds; cuts; abrasions; leg ulcers; inflammatory conditions of the oral and pharyngeal mucosa (mouthwash/gargle); inflammation of the gastric and intestinal mucosa (internal use); cholagogue for hepatobiliary support (internal use).

Original: Flos Calendulae — Calendula officinalis L. (Asteraceae). Active constituents include: flavonoids (isorhamnetin and quercetin glycosides, ~0.3–0.8%), triterpene saponins (oleanolic acid glycosides, ~2–10%), carotenoids (lutein, zeaxanthin, beta-carotene, ~0.01–0.14%), essential oils (~0.02–0.3%), polysaccharides, resins, and bitter glycosides.
title: Calendula (Pot Marigold) Flower

text:
Camphor

Camphor (Camphora), derived from the wood of Cinnamomum camphora, is approved by the German Commission E for external use as a mild rubefacient and mild analgesic for the symptomatic relief of mild muscular pain and as a nasal decongestant when applied to the skin or mucous membranes. Its mechanism of action involves stimulation of cold-sensitive (TRPM8) and warm-sensitive (TRPV1) thermoreceptors in the skin, producing a counterirritant effect and transient sensation of warmth or coolness that modulates local pain perception. In low concentrations it acts as a mild antiseptic and circulatory stimulant on the skin surface. Clinical evidence supporting these uses is largely based on traditional use and pharmacological plausibility rather than modern controlled clinical trials, consistent with Commission E's assessment framework for well-established herbal preparations.

Preparation: External use only. Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: semi-solid and liquid preparations (ointments, creams, liniments, solutions) for topical application to intact skin. Recommended concentration: 10–20% camphor in preparations for musculoskeletal complaints; 1–10% in preparations for nasal decongestion (applied to skin of chest/back, not directly to mucosa in infants). Applied to affected area up to three times daily. Internal use is not approved and is contraindicated. Camphor-containing preparations must not be applied to damaged skin, near the eyes, or to the facial skin of infants and young children due to risk of laryngospasm and neurotoxicity.
Indication: Symptomatic relief of mild muscular pain and rheumatic complaints (external); nasal congestion (external/inhalation); mild circulatory stimulation of the skin.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Camphor (Cinnamomum camphora). Part used: Camphora. Active constituent: Camphor (1,7,7-trimethylbicyclo[2.2.1]heptan-2-one), a bicyclic monoterpene ketone, typically present at high concentrations (≥96% in refined camphor preparations per pharmacopoeial standards).
title: Camphor

text:
Cayenne Pepper / Chili Pepper

The German Commission E approved topical preparations of Capsicum (cayenne pepper fruit) for the treatment of painful muscle spasms in the shoulder, arm, and spine, as well as for rheumatic conditions and neuralgia. The primary mechanism of action is attributed to capsaicin, which initially stimulates and subsequently desensitizes cutaneous nociceptors (C-fiber afferents) by depleting substance P, the principal neuropeptide mediating peripheral pain transmission. Repeated topical application produces a prolonged analgesic and counter-irritant [Rubefaciens] effect by rendering the local nerve endings temporarily insensitive to painful stimuli. Clinical evidence supports short-term efficacy for localized musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain when applied as a standardized cream, ointment, or plaster.

Preparation: Topical use only (internal use is not approved under Commission E for therapeutic purposes). Approved dosage forms include: semi-solid preparations (creams, ointments, gels) and transdermal plasters containing 0.02–0.05% capsaicin. Tinctures for topical use: prepared from Fructus Capsici with a drug-to-solvent ratio corresponding to a final capsaicin content within the above range. Applied to the affected area up to three to four times daily; a treatment-free interval should follow prolonged use to allow sensory recovery. Preparations should not be applied to broken or irritated skin, near eyes, or on mucous membranes.
Indication: Painful muscle spasms (shoulder, arm, spine); rheumatic musculoskeletal disorders; peripheral neuralgia [counter-irritant / topical analgesic indication]

Original: Fructus Capsici (Capsicum annuum L. and related species, family Solanaceae). Key active compounds: capsaicinoids (primarily capsaicin and dihydrocapsaicin), comprising 0.1–1.5% of dry weight; further constituents include carotenoids (capsanthin, capsorubin), flavonoids, and steroidal saponins.
title: Cayenne Pepper / Chili Pepper

text:
Caraway Fruit

Caraway fruit (Fructus Carvi) is approved by the German Commission E for the treatment of dyspeptic complaints, including mild, spasmodic gastrointestinal disorders, feelings of fullness, and flatulence. The therapeutic action is attributed primarily to the volatile oil constituents—carvone and limonene—which exert carminative, antispasmodic, and mild antimicrobial effects on the gastrointestinal tract by relaxing smooth muscle and reducing gas accumulation. Clinical and pharmacological evidence supports the traditional use of caraway as a digestive remedy, and it is frequently combined with peppermint oil (as in fixed combination preparations) for functional dyspepsia. The Commission E assessed the benefit-risk ratio as positive for these indications.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: (1) Crushed or freshly ground dried fruit as an infusion (tea): 1–2 teaspoons (approximately 1.5–6 g) of crushed fruit per cup of boiling water, steeped for 10–15 minutes, taken 2–3 times daily between meals; (2) Essential oil: 3–6 drops per day on a sugar cube or in warm water; (3) Tincture and fluid extracts in equivalent doses; (4) Caraway is also available in compound preparations (e.g., combined with peppermint oil). Average daily dose: 1.5–6 g of the drug or equivalent preparations.
Indication: Dyspeptic complaints; mild spasmodic gastrointestinal disorders; flatulence; feelings of fullness (bloating); functional dyspepsia

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Caraway (Carum carvi). Part used: Fructus Carvi. Key active compounds: volatile essential oil (3–7%), primarily carvone (50–65%) and limonene (20–30%); fixed oils; flavonoids; polysaccharides.
title: Caraway Fruit

text:
Cardamom — Digestive Complaints

According to the German Commission E, cardamom fruit [Fructus Cardamomi] is approved for the symptomatic relief of dyspeptic complaints, including feelings of fullness, flatulence, and mild gastrointestinal spasms. Its therapeutic activity is attributed primarily to the volatile oil fraction, which exerts carminative, mild spasmolytic, and choleretic effects on the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical use is supported by traditional empirical evidence consistent with Commission E positive monograph status, though large-scale controlled clinical trials are limited. The drug is typically used as a component of combination preparations for digestive complaints rather than as a standalone therapeutic agent.

Preparation: Approved dosage forms per German Commission E: comminuted [coarsely ground] or powdered drug for infusions (teas), tinctures, and dry or liquid extracts; also used as a spice-drug in combination preparations. Recommended daily dose: 1.5 g of the whole or freshly crushed fruit (equivalent preparation). Infusion: approximately 1.5 g drug per cup, taken two to three times daily between meals. Tincture and extract doses are standardised to equivalent amounts of volatile oil. Commission E does not specify a maximum dose ceiling beyond the standard therapeutic range.
Indication: ['Dyspeptic complaints', 'Flatulence', 'Feelings of gastric fullness', 'Mild gastrointestinal spasms']

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum). Part used: Fructus Cardamomi. Key active compounds: volatile oil (3–8%), principally 1,8-cineole (20–40%) and α-terpinyl acetate (30–45%), together with fixed oils, starch, and proteins.
title: Cardamom — Digestive Complaints

text:
Cascara Sagrada Bark

Cascara sagrada bark [Cortex Rhamni Purshianae] is approved by the German Commission E as a short-term treatment for constipation. Its primary mechanism of action is dual: the anthraquinone glycosides (principally cascarosides) inhibit stationary colonic motor activity while stimulating propulsive contractions, and simultaneously reduce net fluid and electrolyte absorption in the large intestine, thereby softening stool and accelerating transit. Clinical evidence supports its use for functional constipation in cases where dietary measures and bulk-forming agents have proved insufficient. Use should be limited to short-term application (generally one to two weeks) to avoid habituation, electrolyte disturbance, and secondary hypotonicity of the colon.

Preparation: Oral administration only. Approved dosage forms include: (1) comminuted bark or powdered bark for decoction/infusion; (2) dry extracts and fluid extracts standardised to hydroxyanthracene glycoside content; (3) tablets and capsules containing standardised extracts. Recommended daily dose: the equivalent of 20–30 mg hydroxyanthracene derivatives (calculated as cascaroside A), taken as a single dose in the evening. The smallest effective dose producing comfortable soft-formed stool should always be used. Duration of use should not exceed one to two weeks without medical supervision.
Indication: Short-term symptomatic treatment of occasional constipation [Obstipation]; conditions requiring facilitated defecation (e.g., anal fissures, haemorrhoids, post-anorectal surgery).

Original: Cortex Rhamni Purshianae — dried bark of Rhamnus purshianus DC. (Rhamnaceae). Key active constituents: hydroxyanthracene glycosides (cascarosides A, B, C, D; barbaloin; chrysaloin), comprising not less than 8% total hydroxyanthracene derivatives calculated as cascaroside A on a dry-weight basis.
title: Cascara Sagrada Bark

text:
Cat's Claw Bark (Uncaria tomentosa)

Cat's Claw bark (Cortex Uncariae) is used as a supportive treatment for inflammatory conditions, particularly rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis, and as a general immune system modulator. Its principal active constituents are the pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids (POAs), which have demonstrated immunostimulant and anti-inflammatory properties in vitro and in early clinical studies, partly through inhibition of NF-κB signalling and modulation of cytokine release. The quinovic acid glycosides and polyphenolic tannins contribute additional anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. The German Commission E did not issue a formal positive or negative monograph for this herb within its main published series; the plant is included in reference compilations and assessed under expanded Commission E and ESCOP frameworks, where supportive evidence for anti-inflammatory use is acknowledged but considered preliminary.

Preparation: Oral preparations: dried bark decoction, 1–3 g of powdered bark per cup of water, simmered 15 minutes, taken 1–3 times daily; standardised dry extract capsules or tablets (typically standardised to ≥3% total oxindole alkaloids or ≥1.3% pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids), 250–350 mg extract 2–3 times daily. Duration of use: up to 8 weeks; longer use only under medical supervision. Note: preparations containing significant levels of tetracyclic oxindole alkaloids (TOAs) are considered to antagonise the immunostimulant effects of POAs and should be avoided. Contraindicated in pregnancy, autoimmune disease, organ transplant recipients, and children under 3 years.
Indication: Supportive treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis (anti-inflammatory); adjunctive immune modulation; traditional use in gastrointestinal inflammation.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Cat's Claw (Uncaria tomentosa). Part used: Cortex Uncariae (bark of Uncaria tomentosa [Willd. ex Schult.] DC., family Rubiaceae). Key active compounds: oxindole alkaloids (mitraphylline, isomitraphylline, pteropodine, isopteropodine, speciophylline, uncarine F), pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids (POAs) and tetracyclic oxindole alkaloids (TOAs); also quinovic acid glycosides, tannins (procyanidins), phytosterols (beta-sitosterol, stigmasterol, campesterol), and polyphenols.
title: Cat's Claw Bark (Uncaria tomentosa)

text:
German Chamomile (Matricaria recutita) — Flower Head

German chamomile flower heads (Flos Chamomillae) are approved by the German Commission E for internal use in the treatment of gastrointestinal spasms and inflammatory diseases of the gastrointestinal tract, and for external use on skin and mucous membrane inflammations, including those of the oral cavity and gums, as well as for wound healing and symptomatic relief of ano-genital inflammation. The primary pharmacological activities — anti-inflammatory, antispasmodic, carminative, and mild antimicrobial — are attributed principally to (−)-α-bisabolol and bisabolol oxides, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and 5-lipoxygenase pathways, and to chamazulene, which suppresses leukotriene B4 synthesis; the flavone apigenin additionally binds benzodiazepine receptors, contributing to mild anxiolytic and antispasmodic effects. Topically, the essential oil and flavonoid fractions promote granulation tissue formation and accelerate re-epithelialization in minor wounds and inflammatory skin conditions. Clinical and experimental evidence supports the Commission E approval, with the monograph noting that preparations must meet minimum essential-oil content specifications (≥ 0.3% v/w for the dried flower) to ensure therapeutic equivalence.

Preparation: Internal use — Infusion (tea): 3 g dried flower heads per 150 mL boiling water, steeped covered for 5–10 minutes and strained; taken 3–4 times daily between meals. Fluid extract (1:1, 45% ethanol): 1–3 mL three times daily. Tincture (1:5, 45% ethanol): 3–10 mL three times daily. External use — Semi-solid preparations (creams, ointments) containing 3–10% chamomile extract or a minimum of 0.3% chamazulene for topical application to inflamed skin and mucous membranes. Rinse/gargle solution: 1% fluid extract or infusion from 3–5 g dried flowers in 100 mL water, used several times daily. Bath additive (partial bath or sitz bath for ano-genital use): 50 g dried flower heads or equivalent standardised extract per full bath. Steam inhalation: 6 g dried flower heads per litre of boiling water (no defined upper limit specified in Commission E monograph). All preparations for oral mucosa/gum use (e.g. mouth rinse) should use aqueous or hydroalcoholic extracts at concentrations consistent with the above.
Indication: Primary indications approved by German Commission E: (1) Internal — gastrointestinal spasms; inflammatory and irritative conditions of the gastrointestinal tract (gastritis, enteritis, irritable bowel). (2) External — inflammatory and irritative conditions of skin and mucous membranes (including oral mucositis, gingivitis); wound healing support; symptomatic treatment of ano-genital inflammation (sitz bath); inhalation for upper-respiratory catarrh and inflammation of oral/pharyngeal mucosa.

Original: Source: German Commission E Monographs. Plant: Chamomile German (Matricaria recutita). Part used: Flos Chamomillae. Key active compounds: essential oil (0.3–1.5%), primarily (−)-α-bisabolol and bisabolol oxides A and B; chamazulene (1–15% of essential oil, formed from matricine during steam distillation); apigenin-7-glucoside and other flavonoids (apigenin, luteolin, quercetin); en-yn-dicycloethers (spiroethers); mucilaginous polysaccharides.
title: German Chamomile (Matricaria recutita) — Flower Head
